summary: Specifies a framework for policy-based control over admission control decisions, describing the roles and interactions of the components involved. This is an informational memo.

eli5.summary: This is a map of who decides what when a network is asked to save space for someone.

questions: what is policy based admission control
what is a policy decision point
what is a policy enforcement point
subtitle: A framework for letting network managers decide who may reserve network resources, using a policy server and enforcing routers.

tldr.problem: QoS reservation mechanisms like RSVP check only the request and the available capacity, so providers cannot control who gets better service based on identity, time of day or agreements.
tldr.mechanism: Routers act as Policy Enforcement Points that ask a Policy Decision Point, optionally after a local decision, whether to accept each request, and then enforce the answer.
tldr.outcome: The memo defines the roles, goals and example policies, and lists requirements for the protocol between the two points, but specifies no particular policy or protocol.

facts.label: PDPs expected
facts.value: At least one per administrative domain

today: RFC 2753 is an Informational framework from January 2000 and, per the unit metadata, has not been obsoleted or updated. It does not specify an Internet standard of any kind.

sections.title: Why Admission Needs Policy
sections.content:
Integrated Services and RSVP let applications request a specific quality of service. Admission control in that model only weighs the reservation request against available capacity. It leaves out something managers need: the ability to monitor, control and enforce use of network resources based on policies drawn from user and application identity, bandwidth needs, security and time of day or week.

This memo specifies a framework for policy-based control over admission decisions. It uses RSVP as its main example of a QoS signaling mechanism, but aims to apply to other QoS contexts, including Differentiated Services.
sections.eli5: Having room is not the only question. Sometimes the network also has to ask whether you are allowed to use that room right now.

sections.title: Goals and Requirements
sections.content:
The framework does not define specific policies. It only outlines the elements needed so that many kinds of policy can be carried out. The memo lists these requirements:

  • Preemption: removing an installed reservation to accept a new request.
  • Many policy styles: including bilateral and multilateral agreements and relative priority.
  • Monitoring and accounting: usage and access information usable for billing.
  • Fault tolerance: recovery from failure of decision points and from network partitions.
  • Policy-ignorant nodes (PINs): support must not be mandatory on every node, so policy can be enforced at a subset such as boundary nodes.
  • Scalability: at least as well as RSVP, including for large multicast flows.
  • Security: minimize theft and denial of service, and let PEPs and PDPs verify each other's identity.
sections.eli5: The rules have to allow bumping someone out, keeping count for the bill, surviving breakdowns, and working even if some routers do not know about the rules.

sections.title: PEP, PDP and the Local Decision Point
sections.content:
Two elements do the work. The Policy Enforcement Point (PEP) runs on the network node and enforces decisions. The Policy Decision Point (PDP) usually sits on a remote policy server and makes them. The PDP may use other protocols such as LDAP or SNMP to reach policy databases, authentication and accounting. A node may also have an optional Local Decision Point (LPDP), or the PDP may be co-located with the PEP.

The PEP builds a request from the triggering message plus policy elements. It may first pass a chosen set of elements to the LPDP for a partial result. It then sends the request, all policy elements and that partial result to the PDP, which combines its own result with the partial one and returns the final decision. The PDP is the final authority, and the PEP must enforce its decision.

The PEP MUST contact the PDP even when the request carries no policy objects, so a request cannot dodge policy by leaving them out. A "short circuit" is allowed: if the local result is no, further processing at the PDP can be skipped, though the PDP must still be told of the failure. The PDP may also send asynchronous notifications at any time to change an earlier decision.
sections.eli5: The router is the guard, the policy server is the boss. The guard may check a few simple rules first, but the boss always gets the final say, and the guard must always ask, even when you show no ticket.

sections.title: How an RSVP Router Uses Policy
sections.content:
In an RSVP router, the RSVP module hands requests to its PEP, which consults the LPDP and PDP and passes the decision back. The PDP is stateful and can decide even with no policy objects, using information such as flowspecs.

The PDP can also ask the router to generate policy errors or warnings carried by the QoS signaling protocol. For a PDP error, it states one of two things: either process the message as usual but send an error or warning in the other direction carrying the policy objects, or return an error and do not forward the message.

The memo expects at least one PDP per administrative domain. Policy-capable nodes can range from simple ones that rely on an external PDP for everything to self-sufficient ones that hold both an LPDP and a PDP, which allows staged deployment. Details of RSVP handling are left to RFC 2750 and RFC 2749.
sections.eli5: If the boss says yes but wants to leave a note such as a warning, the router can pass the note along. Different routers can be simple or smart, so a network can upgrade a few at a time.

sections.title: Example Policies
sections.content:
The memo walks through scenarios the framework should support.

  • Time and identity: a group may reserve certain levels only off-peak, or requests may be accepted or denied by credentials.
  • Bilateral agreements: neighboring providers agree on access control and accounting. Boundary nodes add a policy object naming the provider and an account-like identifier, and objects are rewritten at each domain boundary.
  • Priority: a higher-priority reservation can preempt lower-priority ones. Merging priority is the hard part, especially for heterogeneous reservations, where keeping the highest priority works only when reservations are identical.
  • Pre-paid tokens: a policy object carries a card identifier that policy servers decrement, with open questions about charge scope and when to start charging.
  • Sender restrictions: a sender can install state in routers via PATH messages to limit which receivers may reserve, possibly forming closed multicast groups.
sections.eli5: Examples include cheaper hours at night, a prepaid phone card for network speed, VIPs who can bump others, and a sender who says only my friends may join.

sections.title: PEP-PDP Protocol and Security
sections.content:
If the PDP is external, a standardized protocol between PEP and PDP is needed for interoperability. The memo lists requirements: reliability (possibly reusing TCP), small delays, carrying opaque variable-length objects, PEP-initiated two-way transactions, asynchronous notification in both directions, multicast group handling and precise QoS specification.

For security, the channel between policy clients and servers should use an IPSec channel, advisably with both AH and ESP for confidentiality, origin authentication, integrity and replay prevention. For RSVP itself, RSVP MD5 message authentication can secure communication between network elements.
sections.eli5: The guard and the boss should talk in a sealed envelope that nobody can read or fake, and they need to answer quickly and reliably.
